blocks.x: What's changing with Manitoba's $2,000 rent control threshold
The [Province of Manitoba](https://news.gov.mb.ca/news/?archive=&item=75138) is expanding rent regulation for 2027, and the $2,000 rent control threshold is the main change:
The **rent increase guideline** for 2027 is **3%**.
The **exemption threshold** for units rises from **$1,670 to $2,000** per month on January 1, 2027.

Most units renting below that amount are regulated. Units in buildings first occupied after March 7, 2005 are exempt for 20 years from the first occupancy permit or first tenant, whichever came first. Social housing, government-run units, co-op units, non-profit life-lease units and approved rehabilitated units are also exempt.

Other units renting between $1,670 and $2,000 will now be covered by the guideline. Landlords can still apply for an [above-guideline increase](https://www.gov.mb.ca/cca/rtb/landlord/aboveguide.html) to recover part of their eligible capital costs, but approval depends on documentation and the province's rules.

[Since October 30, 2026](https://web2.gov.mb.ca/laws/regs/annual/2026/116.php), capital costs count for 40% less in an above-guideline application: 20%, 15%, 10% or 7.5% of the cost, depending on the item. And from October 20, 2026, a proposed above-guideline increase isn't payable at all until there is a Branch order.
Why it matters now

The rental market is also softening. The average unfurnished one-bedroom asking rent was $1,319 in [liv.rent's October 2026 report](https://liv.rent/blog/?p=69631), after three monthly declines, though still up 1.7% from a year earlier.

Two-bedrooms moved the other way in East Winnipeg, where the average asking rent rose about 8% from September to October, to $1,657. One month's rise after a dip in September is a signal to watch, not proof of a shortage.
For landlords, the combination means:
**Rents are not rising quickly** in many segments.
**Future increases will be capped** for more units.
**The rent at turnover has limits** for regulated units in larger buildings, so it can't simply follow the market.
Our view: upgrade before you re-lease

When a regulated unit turns over, the rule depends on the building. In a complex with four or more units, the new tenant's rent can't be more than the average rent of similar units in that complex. In a complex with three units or fewer, the landlord sets the amount.

A fourplex where the landlord lives in one unit counts as three. Either way, the landlord must give a Notice to New Tenant and send the Branch a copy within 14 days. Units exempt from rent regulation fall outside this rule.

Upgrades don't change those limits. What they can do is help a unit compete. Units that look fresh and well finished tend to lease more easily. Units that look worn may need lower rents or concessions, and in a regulated unit a lower rent can become the base for capped future increases.
That still makes cost-effective upgrades before re-leasing worthwhile, because an empty unit is the easiest time to do the work. The goal is to maximize the unit's appeal at a reasonable cost.
Where interior doors fit in

Interior doors are often overlooked, but they shape how a unit feels. Old hollow-core doors with dents, holes, mismatched hardware and peeling paint make even a freshly painted unit look tired. Replacing them makes a visible difference.
Interior door installation can include:
**Bedroom, bathroom and closet doors,** in a consistent modern style.
**Solid-core doors,** which reduce noise between rooms and feel more substantial.
**New hardware,** such as matching levers and hinges.
**Trim and casing** replacement where damaged.
**Suite entry doors,** which may need to be fire-rated in multi-unit buildings, so check before you replace them.
A turnover upgrade package

Bundled together and scheduled by one contractor, these upgrades leave you with one schedule to manage between tenancies. Where a [kitchen](/services/kitchen-renovations) or [bathroom](/services/bathroom-renovations) needs more than a refresh, treat it as its own project.

Check for asbestos before old flooring or plaster is disturbed. Buildings built or renovated before 1990 are the ones the Province names, and our guide covers [asbestos testing before you renovate](/blog/asbestos-testing-before-renovating-manitoba).
Documentation matters

If landlords plan to seek above-guideline increases for larger capital projects, good records are essential, because a claim can only include costs already paid or billed, and rebates must be declared. Keep itemized invoices, scopes of work and before-and-after photos. Even for smaller upgrades, documentation helps with insurance, tax and future planning.

Landlords should confirm with the Residential Tenancies Branch which costs qualify. Rehabilitation schemes are a separate route. With the Branch's approval, one can exempt a complex or part of it for up to 5 years, or one unit for up to 2 years. Apply before work starts, because the rules limit work done before the first order.
A note on timing

The new threshold applies to rent increases that take effect on or after January 1, 2027, no matter when notice was given. Under the regulation, the test is whether the rent payable on December 31 of the previous year was $2,000 or more. Ask the Residential Tenancies Branch how this applies to a specific unit.

The Branch's FAQ puts it differently, as more than $2,000 a month as of December 31, 2026, so check with the Branch if a unit is at exactly $2,000. Whatever the timing, a well-kept unit can help attract a tenant who stays.
Don't forget common areas

Unit upgrades are more effective when common areas also look cared for. Prospective tenants see the entrance, lobby and hallway before they see the unit. Fresh paint and flooring in common areas support every upgraded unit.
The bottom line

Manitoba's rent rule changes bring more units under the guideline and reduce what capital work can add to an above-guideline application. Landlords who know the turnover rule for their building, and complete cost-effective upgrades before re-leasing, are better placed to lease units and keep good tenants.
